title: Client libraries intake framework for enterprise SDK requests
creator: Marisol Cheng
description:
Purpose: define a repeatable intake and prioritization framework for customer requests that affect client libraries (language bindings, auth patterns, and streaming ergonomics). This ticket codifies how PM will triage inbound asks from sales, CSMs, partners, and open-source contributors so engineering and design get high-confidence, scoped work that aligns to enterprise SLAs and platform constraints.

Context: in H2 2025 we saw growing variability in SDK asks: bespoke auth flows for customers with proprietary identity platforms, differing expectations around streaming APIs between web/mobile/server environments, and requests for new language bindings with low initial usage but high enterprise request volume. Without a consistent rubric, team bandwidth is spent on ad-hoc shipping and maintenance debt.

Goals: (1) create a lightweight intake template for requests, (2) publish a scoring rubric for prioritization that balances customer ROI and long-term maintenance cost, (3) define a small set of supported enterprise auth patterns and streaming primitives we will own, and (4) enumerate the rollout and canary process for any SDK change that impacts authentication or streaming behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Published intake template in Confluence and linked from the SDK support playbook
Scoring rubric v1 documented and used on next 10 inbound SDK requests
List of supported auth patterns (OIDC with refresh, SAML token-exchange, service account flows) agreed with Security and included in SDK pattern docs
Streaming primitive spec (client/server cancellation semantics, backpressure signals, ordered event delivery) approved by runtime and SDK leads
Rollout checklist for SDK changes that touch auth or streaming (canary, telemetry gating, migration guidance) published and added to release process
proposed_workflow: 1) Intake: Sales/CSM/partner creates an intake using the template (customer context, gap, priority, business impact, expected number of customers). 2) Triage: PM team performs initial classification (language request, auth, streaming, bug, docs) within 3 business days. 3) Scoring: apply rubric across customer impact, security complexity, maintenance cost, implementation effort, and strategic alignment. 4) Decision: categorize into Backlog / Quick Win (<=3d) / Epic (>=3w) / Reject. 5) Hand-off: approved items get a scoped PRD, estimate, and engineering assignee before scheduling. 6) Release: follow SDK canary and telemetry gating; inform customers and CSMs of timelines.
decision_rationale: We will prioritize high-security and high-customer-impact requests first (enterprise customers requesting SAML/OIDC flows, token exchange). Language bindings will be prioritized based on a weighted sum of active customers+expected usage+maintenance slope; initial focus is on first-class support for Java, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Go. For streaming ergonomics, we will standardize on a minimal surface: a single unified streaming primitive with explicit cancelation token, optional client-side buffering controls, and deterministic ordering guarantees where the runtime supports it. Trade-offs: narrower surface reduces maintenance but may require minor customer adapter code. Broad support for dozens of languages increases community contributions but also costs; we will use official + community model (official for top 4 languages, community-maintained for others with testing guidance).
